harena-01-c1.text: James Grout. The Roman Gladiator. Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago).
harena-01-c1.quote: They were introduced to Rome in 264 BC, when the sons of Junius Brutus honored their father by matching three pairs of gladiators.
harena-01-c1.claim: In 264 BCE two brothers, Marcus and Decimus Brutus, honoured their dead father in the Forum Boarium, the city's cattle market, by matching three pairs of gladiators.

harena-01-c1.text: Owen Jarus (2024). Did Roman gladiators really fight to the death?. Live Science.
harena-01-c1.quote: tomb paintings dating to the fourth century B.C. at the site of Paestum, a Lucanian city in Italy that eventually came under Roman rule, show that the "gladiators are receiving terrible wounds,"
harena-01-c1.claim: The physical evidence points south as well: tomb paintings of the fourth century BCE at Paestum, a Lucanian city in southern Italy, show fighters receiving terrible, plainly fatal wounds.

harena-01-c2.text: James Grout. The Roman Gladiator. Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago).
harena-01-c2.quote: Elected aedile in 65 BC, Julius Caesar commemorated his father, who had died twenty years before, with a display of 320 pairs of gladiators in silvered armor
harena-01-c2.claim: Elected aedile in 65 BCE, he honoured his father, who had died twenty years before, with 320 pairs of gladiators in silvered armour.

harena-01-c3.text: James Grout. The Roman Gladiator. Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago).
harena-01-c3.quote: Gladiatorial games were presented perhaps ten or twelve days each year and often coincided with the celebration of the Saturnalia.
harena-01-c3.claim: In Rome they ran perhaps ten or twelve days a year, often around the Saturnalia festival.

harena-02-c1.text: Mark Cartwright (2018). Colosseum: Rome's Great Flavian Amphitheatre. World History Encyclopedia.
harena-02-c1.quote: The construction of the Colosseum was begun in 72 CE in the reign of Vespasian on the site that was once the lake and gardens of Emperor Nero's Golden House.
harena-02-c1.claim: Vespasian began the building in the early 70s CE on the site of the lake and gardens of Nero's Golden House.

harena-02-c2.text: Mark Cartwright (2018). Colosseum: Rome's Great Flavian Amphitheatre. World History Encyclopedia.
harena-02-c2.quote: opened for business in 80 CE in the reign of Titus, Vespasian's eldest son, with a one hundred day gladiator spectacular
harena-02-c2.claim: Titus opened the amphitheatre in 80 CE with games that lasted a hundred days.

harena-02-c2.text: Cassius Dio, translated by Earnest Cary (1925). Roman History, Book LXVI. LacusCurtius (Loeb Classical Library text).
harena-02-c2.quote: There was a battle between cranes and also between four elephants; animals both tame and wild were slain to the number of nine thousand
harena-02-c2.claim: The historian Cassius Dio, a senator who lived about a century later, lists the highlights: a battle between cranes, another between four elephants, and animals tame and wild "slain to the number of nine thousand".

harena-02-c3.text: Archaeology Newsroom (2015). How ancient Romans lifted wild animals into the Colosseum. Archaeology Wiki.
harena-02-c3.quote: Further investigation revealed that there were somewhere between 24 and 28 lifts specifically designed to transport up to 600 pounds each—the average weight of two lions.
harena-02-c3.claim: By one count there were between 24 and 28 lifts, each able to raise about 600 pounds, roughly two lions.

harena-03-c1.text: James Grout. The Roman Gladiator. Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago).
harena-03-c1.quote: Free men also volunteered to be gladiators (auctorati) and, by the end of the Republic, comprised half the number who fought.
harena-03-c1.claim: By the end of the Republic, by one modern estimate, free men made up half of those who fought.

harena-03-c2.text: Archaeology Magazine (2012). Gladiator Gym Goes Virtual: Top 10 Discoveries of 2011. Archaeology Magazine.
harena-03-c2.quote: gladiator school, the fourth largest ever found in the world, located just west of the largest amphitheater outside of Rome, is a self-enclosed complex that includes an inner courtyard, circular training area, living quarters, and a cemetery
harena-03-c2.claim: The fourth-century school, the fourth largest ever found, is a self-enclosed complex with an inner courtyard, a circular training area, living quarters and a cemetery, plus under-floor heating and a bathing area.

harena-03-c3.text: James Grout. The Roman Gladiator. Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago).
harena-03-c3.quote: It was important that these different types of gladiators be appropriately paired, the advantage of one being compensated for by the strength of the other.
harena-03-c3.claim: Fighters were meant to be evenly matched but not identically armed, so the advantage of one was offset by the strength of the other.

harena-04-c1.text: Owen Jarus (2024). Did Roman gladiators really fight to the death?. Live Science.
harena-04-c1.quote: gladiator fights painted on the walls of Pompeii say that out of 5 fights, one ended with the death of the loser," Manas said, adding that this death rate probably remained similar during the second century
harena-04-c1.claim: In the first century CE, he finds, about one fight in five ended with the death of the loser, and the rate probably stayed similar in the second century.

harena-04-c1.text: Owen Jarus (2024). Did Roman gladiators really fight to the death?. Live Science.
harena-04-c1.quote: if a gladiator was returned severely injured — or killed outright — the lease of the gladiator would be converted to a sale [and] the price could increase by something like 50 times the original contract cost
harena-04-c1.claim: Magistrates rented gladiators from their owners, and according to Virginia Campbell of the Open University, surviving contracts suggest that a gladiator returned badly injured or dead turned the lease into a sale, at a price perhaps fifty times the original fee.

harena-04-c3.text: Sandra Lösch, Negahnaz Moghaddam, Karl Grossschmidt, Daniele U. Risser, Fabian Kanz (2014). Stable Isotope and Trace Element Studies on Gladiators and Contemporary Romans from Ephesus (Turkey, 2nd and 3rd Ct. AD) - Implications for Differences in Diet. PLOS ONE.
harena-04-c3.quote: In 1993, a gladiator cemetery was discovered in Ephesus, Turkey
harena-04-c3.claim: Then, in 1993, a gladiator cemetery was discovered at Ephesus, the great Roman city near the Aegean coast of Turkey.

harena-04-c3.text: T. J. U. Thompson, D. Errickson, Christine McDonnell, Malin Holst, Anwen Caffell, John Pearce, Rebecca L. Gowland (2025). Unique osteological evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat in Roman Britain. PLOS ONE.
harena-04-c3.quote: Eleven of these bodies showed evidence of well-healed antemortem cranial trauma, while ten had cranial injuries incurring around the time of death
harena-04-c3.claim: Eleven showed well-healed injuries from earlier fights, and ten had injuries received around the time of death, made by both blunt and sharp force and consistent with arena combat.

harena-05-c1.text: Sandra Lösch, Negahnaz Moghaddam, Karl Grossschmidt, Daniele U. Risser, Fabian Kanz (2014). Stable Isotope and Trace Element Studies on Gladiators and Contemporary Romans from Ephesus (Turkey, 2nd and 3rd Ct. AD) - Implications for Differences in Diet. PLOS ONE.
harena-05-c1.quote: Their consumption of barley led to the derogatory nickname “hordearii” (barley eaters)
harena-05-c1.claim: Pliny the Elder called gladiators hordearii, "barley eaters", and it was not a compliment.

harena-05-c1.text: Sandra Lösch, Negahnaz Moghaddam, Karl Grossschmidt, Daniele U. Risser, Fabian Kanz (2014). Stable Isotope and Trace Element Studies on Gladiators and Contemporary Romans from Ephesus (Turkey, 2nd and 3rd Ct. AD) - Implications for Differences in Diet. PLOS ONE.
harena-05-c1.quote: All individuals consumed C3 plants like wheat and barley as staple food.
harena-05-c1.claim: Everyone, gladiator or not, lived mainly on C3 plants like wheat and barley, and the gladiators' carbon, nitrogen and sulphur values did not differ significantly from those of ordinary townspeople.

harena-05-c2.text: Sandra Lösch, Negahnaz Moghaddam, Karl Grossschmidt, Daniele U. Risser, Fabian Kanz (2014). Stable Isotope and Trace Element Studies on Gladiators and Contemporary Romans from Ephesus (Turkey, 2nd and 3rd Ct. AD) - Implications for Differences in Diet. PLOS ONE.
harena-05-c2.quote: Since the Sr/Ca-ratio reflects the main Ca-supplier in the diet, the elevated values of the gladiators might suggest a frequent use of a plant ash beverage, as mentioned in ancient texts.
harena-05-c2.claim: Since the Sr/Ca ratio follows the main source of calcium in the diet, a regular ash drink would push it up, and the team calculated that even one gram of plant ash a day would be enough.

harena-05-c3.text: T. J. U. Thompson, D. Errickson, Christine McDonnell, Malin Holst, Anwen Caffell, John Pearce, Rebecca L. Gowland (2025). Unique osteological evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat in Roman Britain. PLOS ONE.
harena-05-c3.quote: An exceptional feature of this cemetery was the very high proportion of decapitation burials (approximately 70% of those with sufficient preservation to ascertain this
harena-05-c3.claim: About 70 per cent of the skeletons well enough preserved to tell had been decapitated, against a usual 5 to 6 per cent in Roman Britain, and most heads had been cut off from behind, a method more often linked with execution.

harena-05-c3.text: T. J. U. Thompson, D. Errickson, Christine McDonnell, Malin Holst, Anwen Caffell, John Pearce, Rebecca L. Gowland (2025). Unique osteological evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat in Roman Britain. PLOS ONE.
harena-05-c3.quote: Thus, we present the first physical evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat from the Roman period seen anywhere in Europe.
harena-05-c3.claim: They called it the first physical evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat from the Roman period anywhere in Europe.

harena-06-c1.text: James Grout. Pollice Verso. Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago).
harena-06-c1.quote: There is no clear textual evidence for the position of the thumb, and the Latin does not admit to precise understanding.
harena-06-c1.claim: The ancient texts are far less clear.

harena-06-c1.text: Phoenix Art Museum (2024). Pollice Verso. Phoenix Art Museum.
harena-06-c1.quote: a “thumbs down” was a signal that a defeated gladiator should be condemned to death (likely influenced by Ridley Scott’s feature film Gladiator), there are no historical records that confirm this
harena-06-c1.claim: Phoenix Art Museum, which bought the painting in 1968, says plainly that no historical records confirm the gesture.

harena-06-c2.text: Suetonius, translated by J. C. Rolfe (1914). The Life of Claudius. LacusCurtius (Loeb Classical Library text).
harena-06-c2.quote: and after that all of them refused to fight, maintaining that they had been pardoned
harena-06-c2.claim: The fighters chose to understand it as a pardon and refused to fight, until the emperor, after hesitating over whether to destroy them all, bullied them into it.

harena-06-c2.text: Joshua J. Mark (2016). The Spartacus Revolt. World History Encyclopedia.
harena-06-c2.quote: These narratives inspired later artists to present Spartacus as a freedom fighter battling the might of Rome to end slavery even though none of the ancient accounts support this conclusion.
harena-06-c2.claim: What the sources do not show is a crusade against slavery.

harena-06-c3.text: Carole Raddato (2015). Female Gladiators. World History Encyclopedia.
harena-06-c3.quote: This marble relief commemorates the honourable release from service (missio) of two women fighters, "Amazon" (named after the female warriors) and "Achilia" (named after the Greek hero Achilles).
harena-06-c3.claim: The relief commemorates their honourable release from service, which they won after a series of outstanding performances.

harena-06-c3.text: Mark Cartwright (2018). Roman Gladiator. World History Encyclopedia.
harena-06-c3.quote: It is also of note that until their outlaw by Septimius Severus in 200 CE, women were permitted to fight as gladiators.
harena-06-c3.claim: Women were permitted to fight until Septimius Severus outlawed it in 200 CE.

harena-07-c1.text: T. J. U. Thompson, D. Errickson, Christine McDonnell, Malin Holst, Anwen Caffell, John Pearce, Rebecca L. Gowland (2025). Unique osteological evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat in Roman Britain. PLOS ONE.
harena-07-c1.quote: Sodalitates (corporations) of animal hunters like the Telegeni, attested in Tunisia, make for plausible sources of experienced personnel
harena-07-c1.claim: Corporations of animal hunters like the Telegenii, known from Tunisia, may have supplied the experts.

harena-07-c2.text: Peter T. Struck (2010). Greatest of All Time. Lapham's Quarterly.
harena-07-c2.quote: Twenty-four years of winnings brought Diocles—likely an illiterate man whose signature move was the strong final dash—the staggering sum of 35,863,120 sesterces in prize money.
harena-07-c2.claim: Over 24 years he won 35,863,120 sesterces in prize money.

harena-07-c3.text: Mark Cartwright (2017). The Hippodrome of Constantinople. World History Encyclopedia.
harena-07-c3.quote: Justinian was not to be so easily pushed from his throne, though, and his generals Belisarius and Mundus ruthlessly quashed the revolt by slaughtering 30,000 of the perpetrators inside the Hippodrome.
harena-07-c3.claim: Justinian's generals Belisarius and Mundus then slaughtered 30,000 people inside the Hippodrome.

harena-07-c3.text: Philip Schaff. History of the Christian Church, Volume III: Abolition of Gladiatorial Shows. Christian Classics Ethereal Library.
harena-07-c3.quote: For there is no law of Honorius extant on the subject.
harena-07-c3.claim: Yet no law of Honorius on the subject survives, so the story may compress a slower decline.
